questions.prompt: Why does Daybook treat a backup file as hostile input, and what makes the import atomic without a database?

keyPoints.text: Even a file the user exported themselves counts as an input boundary.
keyPoints.quote: A file is an input boundary, even when the user exported it from their own computer.

keyPoints.text: Parsing only proves the JSON is well-formed, not that it means anything.
Structurally valid JSON can still be the wrong domain object.
keyPoints.quote: an array of numbers is valid JSON but is not an application list

keyPoints.text: The format/version envelope exists for forward compatibility.
keyPoints.quote: gives future migrations a version to branch on

keyPoints.text: Validation finishes before persistence so partial saves are impossible.
keyPoints.quote: invalid row 500 cannot leave the first 499 rows saved

keyPoints.text: The atomic unit is a single key-value write of the whole array.
keyPoints.quote: Atomicity here is one key-value write

keyPoints.text: Import replaces the stored list outright, and the UI says so.
keyPoints.quote: Import is replacement rather than merge

questions.prompt: What is an invariant here, and how do you turn the backup feature's promises into tests?

keyPoints.text: An invariant holds both before and after the operation under test.
keyPoints.quote: must remain true before and after an operation

keyPoints.text: Whole-app claims are untestable; the statement must be observable.
The feature's concrete promise covers both parse and host-write failure.
keyPoints.quote: A failed parse or rejected host write leaves the displayed applications unchanged.

keyPoints.text: Each promise becomes a state table with four fixed columns.
keyPoints.quote: initial state, input, expected final state and expected feedback

keyPoints.text: Tables should include a rejection and a repeated action.
keyPoints.quote: one rejected input and one retry/repeated action

keyPoints.text: A good invariant survives swapping the storage implementation.
keyPoints.quote: even if the implementation changes from an array to a database

questions.prompt: Distinguish validation from normalization in this importer, and explain why await and try blocks do not provide atomicity.

keyPoints.text: Validation refuses what the operation cannot accept.
keyPoints.quote: Validation rejects values the operation cannot accept.

keyPoints.text: Normalization is the harmless half, such as trimming a comparison string.
keyPoints.quote: Trimming a comparison string is normalization

keyPoints.text: Neither step is allowed to fabricate data.
keyPoints.quote: Neither operation should silently invent facts.

keyPoints.text: Saving just the valid subset of a malformed batch is forbidden unless it is explicit policy.
keyPoints.quote: do not quietly save only the convenient subset

keyPoints.text: Awaiting a promise only gives the caller a place to handle rejection.
keyPoints.quote: does not make it infallible or atomic

keyPoints.text: Grouping calls in one try block is not a transaction.
keyPoints.quote: block does not create a database transaction

keyPoints.text: Daybook gets its atomicity from the single storage.set in commitJobBackup.
